parole.significato: -ise (suffix used in loanwords from French to form abstract nouns of quality or function)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -ise, from Old French -ise, from Latin -itia. Doublet of -ezza and -izia.
Borrowed from French -ose, from Latin -ōsus (whence also -oso).
Borrowed from French agir, itself borrowed from Latin agere.
Borrowed from French allier, itself from Latin alligāre. Doublet of the inherited allegare.
Borrowed from French allègre, from Latin alacer (“lively; happy, cheerful”). Compare the doublet alacre.

parole.significato: apanage (grant (especially by a sovereign) of land (or other source of revenue) as a birthright)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French apanage, derived from apaner (“to provide with a dowry, to dowry”), derived from Vulgar Latin *appānāre, *adpānāre, derived from Classical Latin pānis (“bread”).
Borrowed from French approcher, from Late Latin appropiāre.

parole.significato: are, measurement of area (100 square metres)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French are, from Latin ārea. Doublet of area and aia.

1829, borrowed from French harpagon, as if named after Arpagone (“Harpagon”), the protagonist of Molière's The Miser (1668), whose original name Harpagon is an adaptation of Latin harpagō, gen. harpagōnis (“grappling hook, grappling iron”), from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē, “hook”), from ἁρπάζω (h

From French, from Late Latin arepennis (“surface of a field”), from Gaulish *are-penno- (“end, extremity of a field”); the first element is from Proto-Celtic *(p)ari-, *are, from Proto-Indo-European *per-; the second element, *penis (“head, tip”) is of uncertain origin, but probably related to *kʷen
Borrowed from French assembler, from Latin assimulāre. Doublet of assimilare.

parole.significato: to make sleepy, to make drowsy
parole.testo: Borrowed from French assoupir, re-Latinized from Old French assouvir, from Vulgar Latin *assōpīre, from Latin sōpīre (“to put to sleep”).

parole.significato: to give permission; to warrant or authorize
parole.testo: Borrowed from French autoriser, from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre. Doublet of ottriare.
Borrowed from French aviateur, ultimately from Latin avis (“bird”).
Borrowed from French avulsif, derived from Latin āvulsus (“torn off”), perfect passive participle of āvellō.
Borrowed from French action.

parole.significato: a washtub for clothes, formerly used on ships
parole.testo: Borrowed from French baille, from Late Latin baiula [aquae] (“carrier [of water]”), from a feminine form of Latin baiulus (“carrier, porter”).
Unadapted borrowing from French béton (“concrete”), from Latin bitūmen (“asphalt”). Doublet of bitume.
From French billet, from Old French billette, derived from Latin bulla (“document”).
Borrowed from French bombarde.
Borrowed from French bouteille.
Unadapted borrowing from French bouquet. Doublet of boschetto.
Borrowed from French broche.
From French boudin (“blood pudding”), from Vulgar Latin *botellinus, from Latin botellus (small sausage).
Borrowed from French calorifère (“heater, radiator”), adaptation made using Latin calor (“warmth, heat; glow”) + -fer (“-bearing, -carrying, -bringing”). By surface analysis, from calori- + -fero.
Borrowed from French carline, from Medieval Latin carlina, probably from cardina, a diminutive of Latin carduus (“thistle”), with influence from Carolus Magnus due to an association with Charlemagne.
Borrowed from French champagne, from Champagne, from Late Latin campania. Doublet of campagna.
Borrowed from French charme, from Latin carmen (“song, recitement, incantation”).

Unadapted borrowing from French chef (“head; chief”), from Middle French chief, from Old French chief, from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *káput. Doublet of capo.
From French chambellan, from Old French chamberlein, Medieval Latin camerlingus, from Frankish. Doublet of camerlengo. See also Old French chambre for details on the sound change from Latin camera.
Borrowed from French chenille, from Latin canīcula. Doublet of canicola.
Borrowed from French coalition, from Medieval Latin coalitiōnem (“association”).
Borrowed from French contention or Latin contentiōnem. By surface analysis, contenere + -zione.
Borrowed from French contrôle.
Borrowed from French conscrit, from Latin cōnscrīptus.

Borrowed from French crétin (“fool”), from Alpine French crestin (“Christian”), from Latin Christianus, from Ancient Greek Χριστιανός (Khristianós, “Christian”), from Χριστός (Khristós, “Christ”) (+ -ιανός (-ianós, “-ian”)), from χριστός (khristós, “anointed”), from χρίειν (khríein, “to anoint; to r
Unadapted borrowing from French croissant, present participle of verb croître (“to grow”). Doublet of crescente.
Borrowed from French coucher (“to lay down, to put to bed”), from Middle French coucher, from Old French couchier, from Latin collocāre (“to place, put, assemble”).
Borrowed from French décor.
Borrowed from French déféquer, from Latin dēfaecāre.
Borrowed from French déporter, from Latin dēportāre.
Borrowed from French destituer, from Latin dēstituō.

parole.significato: being a statutory provision not mandatory to the parties, as in ius dispositivum
parole.testo: Borrowed from French dispositif, from Latin dispositus, perfect passive participle of dispōnō.

parole.significato: long robe shaped as a cloak with a hood, worn at masked balls
parole.testo: Borrowed from French domino, from Medieval Latin dominō, dative of Latin dominus (“lord, master”); possibly from the liturgical phrase benedīcāmus Dominō (literally “let us bless the Lord”).
Borrowed from French émulsion, from New Latin ēmulsiōnem, based on Latin ēmulgeō (“to milk out, extract”).
From French épiglottal, derived from épiglotte, from Late Latin epiglottis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιγλωττίς (epiglōttís), derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).

Borrowed from French filtre, from Medieval Latin filtrum, from Frankish *filtir, plural of *filt, from Proto-West Germanic *felt (“felt”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *peld- (“something beaten or compressed; felt”), derived from the root *pelh₂- (“to beat; to push”).
Borrowed from French forge, from Old French forge, from earlier faverge, from Latin fabrica, derived from faber (“forger, smith”). Doublet of fabbrica.
Borrowed from French franc.
Borrowed from French frange, from Late Latin fimbria, from Latin fimbriae. Compare Sicilian frinza.
Unadapted borrowing from French frigidaire, from a genericized trademark based on Latin frīgidārium, derived from frīgidus (“cold, cool”). Doublet of frigidario.

parole.significato: frigorie (unit of rate of extraction of heat)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French frigorie, derived from Latin frīgus (“cold, coldness”).
Borrowed from French fronde (“slingshot; opposition”), ultimately from Latin funda (“sling, slingshot”), probably through a contracted, metathesized diminutive form (Vulgar Latin *flunda ← *fundula).

Borrowed from French garçon, from Old French garçon, from Medieval Latin garciō, from earlier *warciō, from Frankish *wrakkijō (“mercenary; servant”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile; warrior”). Cognate with Sicilian jarzuni.
Borrowed from French jansénisme, derived from Latin Jānsenius, Latinized form of Dutch Jansen (a surname).
Borrowed from French janséniste, derived from Latin Jānsenius, Latinized form of Dutch Jansen (a surname).
Borrowed from French javelot, from Vulgar Latin *gabalottus (“spear”), derived from Gaulish *gabalos.
Borrowed from French gorge, from Middle French gorge, from Old French gorge, from Late Latin gurga, related to Latin gurges (“whirlpool”).
Borrowed from French hôtel, from Middle French hostel (“hostel”, “inn”), from Old French ostel (“shelter”), from Latin hospitālis (“pertaining to hospitality”). Doublet of ospedale and ospitale.

parole.significato: to stack, to pile up (boxes, books, hay bales, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French empiler (“to pile up”), from pile (“pile”), from Latin pīla.
Borrowed from French incolore, from Medieval Latin incolōrem, from in- + color.
Borrowed from French intermédiaire, from Latin intermedius.

parole.significato: to make out; to catch a glimpse of
parole.testo: Borrowed from French entrevoir, from Vulgar Latin *intervidēre.
Borrowed from French lame, from Latin lāmina. Doublet of lamina.
From French laisse, from laisser (“to leave”), from Old French laissier, from Latin laxāre (“to expand, make wide”).
Borrowed from French légiférer, from Latin lēgĭfer (“legislator”).
Borrowed from French linge (“linen”), from Latin līneus.
Borrowed from French malique, from Latin mālum.
From French margotte, itself from Latin mergus (“vine-layer”).

Remade from or influenced by French métis, from Late Latin mixtīcius, from Latin mixtus. Cf. the older form mesticcio and also misticcio. The archaic variants mestizo, mestizzo were taken from Spanish mestizo.
Borrowed from French meute, from Middle French meute, from Old French meute, muete, from Vulgar Latin *movita, feminine of *movitus, from the perfect passive participle form of moveō (“to move”).

parole.significato: any member of the Oriolus taxonomic genus
parole.testo: Probably via French oriol, from Latin aureolus (“golden”), derived from aurum (“gold”).
Borrowed from French ouverture, Old French overture, from Vulgar Latin *opertūra, from Latin apertūra. Doublet of apertura, a borrowing from Latin.
Borrowed from French parcelle, from Late Latin particella, diminutive of Latin particula. Doublet of particella and particola.
Borrowed from French péricarpe, from New Latin pericarpium, from Ancient Greek περικάρπιον (perikárpion, “pod, husk, shell”).
Borrowed from French pieuvre, ultimately from Latin polypus, Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous).
From French planer, derived from plain, from Latin plānus (“level”, “flat”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *pleh₂- (“flat”).
Borrowed from French propulsif, from Latin prōpulsus.
Borrowed from French quartier, from Latin quartārium (“fourth part”).

parole.significato: to expel (from a group, institution, etc.) (typically as a disciplinary measure)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French radier, from Medieval Latin radiāre (“to expunge, to delete”), a false relatinization of Old French roier (“to draw a line, to cross out”) (modern French rayer), from roie (“line, ridge between furrows”), from Vulgar Latin *riga, probably from Gaulish *rica (“furrow”).
Borrowed from French ragoût, from Middle French ragoûter (“to awaken the appetite”), from goût (“taste”), from Latin gustus. See also gusto (“taste”) and its derivations.

Unadapted borrowing from French ruche, from Middle French rusche, from Old French rusche, from Early Medieval Latin rusca (“bark”), borrowed from Gaulish rūsca, from Proto-Celtic *rūskos (“bark”), from *rukskos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewk- (“to dig up”), from *Hrew- (“to tear out, dig out”).
Via French saponine from Latin sapō, sapon
Borrowed from French scolaire, from Late Latin scholāris.
Borrowed from French seine, from Late Latin sagēna, from Ancient Greek σαγήνη (sagḗnē).
Borrowed from French systématique (adjective), from Late Latin systematicus, from Ancient Greek συστηματικός (sustēmatikós), from σύστημᾰ (sústēmă).

parole.significato: to be drawn by lot, to be produced by drawing lots
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sortir, from Latin sortīrī (“to draw lots”).
Borrowed from French style, itself borrowed from Latin stilus. Doublet of stelo and stilo, which Italian inherited and borrowed from Latin respectively.

From supporto + -are (productive suffix), borrowed from French support, from the verb supporter, ultimately from Latin supportāre, from sub- (“under”) + portāre (“to carry”). Doublet of sopportare, which is inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from French support, from the verb supporter, ultimately from Latin supportāre.
Borrowed from French tophus, from Latin tophus, tofus (“tuff”).

parole.significato: train (connected sequence of people or things)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French train.
Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbinem.

Borrowed from French ultramontain, from Medieval Latin ultrāmontānus. By surface analysis, from ultramontano. It was originally used to describe non-Italian supporters of the Pope, as they where "beyond the mountains" from Rome.
Borrowed from French vacance, derived from Latin vacantia (“emptiness, leisure”).
Borrowed from French variété (“variety”), from Latin varietātem.
Borrowed from French vélocipède, composed of Latin vēlōci- (“swift”) + pēs, pedem (“foot”).
From French vidimer, itself from Latin vidĭmus (“we have seen”). Compare Piedmontese vidimé, German vidimieren.
Borrowed from French chambre, from Old French chambre, cambre, from Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρᾱ (kamárā). Doublet of camera. Cognate with Sicilian giammra.
